questions.q: Name three supporting characters from "vkyks&vk¡èkkfj" and state one defining action or speech for each that reveals their attitude toward the protagonist.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Rakhi — asks "रक्रीक, तू यहाँ क्या करती है?" showing suspicion; (2) Rakhi's husband — says "मैं तुम्हारी कहानी छपवाऊँगा" showing encouragement; (3) Vkdk'k — brings food to the protagonist saying "माँ ने भेजा है" showing care across class lines. A wrong answer that lists only names without textual evidence reveals the student confuses character identification with character analysis.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Rakhi's attitude toward the protagonist changes from the beginning to the middle of the narrative, and identify the specific incident that marks this shift.
questions.a: Correct answer: Initially Rakhi interrogates the protagonist ("तू यहाँ कैसे आई?"), monitoring her movements. The shift occurs when the protagonist begins writing—Rakhi then asks her to read aloud, offers paper, and says "तू बहुत अच्छा लिखती है." A wrong answer describing only the final relationship misses the power dynamic reversal: literacy becomes the lever that forces Rakhi to recognize the protagonist's humanity.

questions.q: The text describes Vkdk'k (the watchman's son) bringing food to the protagonist. Using this incident, explain how a minor character can embody a thematic contradiction in the narrative.
questions.a: Correct answer: Vkdk'k belongs to the same working class as the protagonist, yet his mother sends food to her—an act of solidarity that contradicts the class-based exploitation the protagonist faces from employers. This mirrors the text's central tension: the poor sustain each other while the wealthy extract labor. A wrong answer that only summarizes the plot event fails to connect the character's action to the theme of class solidarity versus class oppression.

questions.q: Compare how Rakhi's husband and Tsbw each respond to the protagonist's writing. What does this comparison reveal about gender and class positions in the text?
questions.a: Correct answer: Rakhi's husband (educated, male, employer-class) offers public validation—"मैं तुम्हारी कहानी छपवाऊँगा"—exerting institutional power. Tsbw (female, fellow worker) responds with private recognition—"तू तो हमारी आवाज़ बन गई"—exerting communal solidarity. The contrast shows that empowerment operates differently across class and gender: the patriarchal gatekeeper grants access to public sphere; the peer affirms identity within the private sphere. A wrong answer treating both responses as "support" flattens the structural analysis.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Lquhy (the previous domestic worker) functions only as a foil to highlight the protagonist's resilience." Defend or refute using textual evidence.
questions.a: Correct answer: Refute. Lquhy is not merely a foil—she is a warning. When Lquhy says "मैं यहाँ नहीं रहूँगी" and leaves, she demonstrates that exit is possible but costly. The protagonist stays not because she is "stronger" but because she has children to feed and no alternative shelter. Lquhy's departure sharpens the protagonist's dilemma: resistance risks destitution. A wrong answer accepting the foil claim reduces a structural constraint to a character contrast.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from the perspective of Je.k (the younger son) describing the day he discovers the protagonist can read and write. Use textual details to make it authentic.
questions.a: Criteria for a strong answer: (1) Uses child's voice—simple sentences, concrete sensory details (smell of ink, sound of pages turning); (2) References a specific textual moment (e.g., protagonist reading a letter aloud); (3) Shows Je.k's confusion turning to respect, not adult analysis; (4) Ends with a child's question ("क्या तू मुझे भी सिखाएगी?"). A weak answer writes in adult voice, invents events not in text, or makes Je.k articulate class theory.
